summary:
The Earth Information Jukebox, an interactive web application that transforms Earth observation data and satellite imagery into an audiovisual experience. Users navigate a three-dimensional Earth from orbit toward ground level, explore satellite imagery and terrain, and activate sonification to hear visual patterns or changes in scientific measurements.

The application presents NASA and partner datasets, including atmospheric carbon dioxide, global mean sea level, surface temperature anomalies, Arctic sea-ice extent, and ocean and air temperatures. In its scientific timeline, measured values are mapped to sound properties such as pitch and stereo position. Users can play, pause, and scrub through time. A comparison feature lets users examine two environmental indicators together, supported by normalized trajectories, correlation information, and a data table. The interface explains the sonification method, data provenance, and scientific limitations.

The project addresses the Earth Information Jukebox challenge by making Earth science explorable through sight, sound, and interaction rather than charts alone. This matters because climate trends can be difficult to interpret, especially for non-specialists and people who benefit from auditory access. Connecting datasets with an engaging, transparent experience can support science communication, learning, and curiosity about our changing planet. It is an independent prototype, not an official NASA product.
details:
The Earth Information Jukebox is an interactive web application developed to transform complex Earth science data and satellite imagery into an engaging visual and audio experience. It allows users to explore a 3D representation of Earth, zoom from orbital views to ground-level imagery, and listen to environmental data through scientific sonification. The application uses authentic datasets from NASA, NOAA, and earth.gov, covering important environmental indicators such as atmospheric CO₂, global temperature anomalies, sea-level changes, Arctic sea ice, and ocean temperatures. It converts scientific measurements into sound properties such as pitch and stereo positioning, allowing users to hear how environmental conditions change over time. Users can explore historical timelines, compare two environmental metrics, examine numerical data, and understand the mathematical principles behind the generated sounds.

The project provides an alternative way to understand complex scientific information, improves accessibility through auditory experiences, encourages environmental awareness, and makes climate science more engaging for students, researchers, educators, and the general public. Its intended impact is to make Earth observation data easier to explore, interpret, and communicate while encouraging informed discussions about climate change and planetary health.

The project was created using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, CesiumJS, Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles, OpenStreetMap, Nominatim, and the Web Audio API, with deployment on Vercel. During development, our team considered scientific accuracy, authentic data provenance, accessibility, usability, audio clarity, performance, responsive design, and transparency. We also incorporated scientific limitations and data-source information to ensure that the experience remains educational, meaningful, and responsible.

Our vision is to make Earth not just visible, but audible.
